title.en: Kunigseq's Flight Down to the Underworld
title.zh: 庫尼格塞克下行冥界記

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kunigseq', eBook #28932

summary.en: The wizard Kunigseq flies through the floor down to the underworld, where the dead live in a land of sun and smooth seas. His dead mother and brother welcome him but warn him against eating, lest he never return; he promises to send them ice for their thirst and comes back to earth. When his son then dies, Kunigseq eats guillemot and raven — the eaten spirit-food of farewell — and rows out to sea to die.
summary.zh: 巫師庫尼格塞克穿地飛降冥界，死者居於有太陽平海之鄉。亡母亡弟相迎，卻誡其勿食，否則不得歸返；他允諾送冰解冥界之渴，重返人間。其子病亡後，庫尼格塞克先後吞食海鳩與渡鴉——死亡之食——遂乘皮艇出海而逝。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district angakok (shaman) spirit-flight narrative recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The angakok seance is described as historical practice; presented as archival record.

passages.text: Kunigseq the wizard prepared a descent to the underworld: the floor was swilled with salt water to drive away the smell that might frighten his helping spirits. Calling them, he passed downward through the floor without moving his body. On the way a weed-covered reef was too slippery to pass until his helping spirit lay down beside it and he walked over on the spirit's back. Far down, the land is level, the hills are small, and there is sun and a sky like that on earth. He heard a cry: 'Here comes Kunigseq,' and saw children fishing for greyfish by a little river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kunigseq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before reaching the houses he met his dead mother, who had gone out gathering berries; she tried again and again to kiss him, but his helping spirit thrust her aside — 'He is only here on a visit.' When she offered berries the spirit warned him: 'If you eat of them, you will never return.' He caught sight of his dead brother; his mother urged him to stay — look at the great stores of dried meat, the smooth sea, no snow, a beautiful open sea where two kayaks rowed and laughed, darting birds. 'I will come again when I die,' said Kunigseq. On a little island lay the drying kayaks of men who had just lost their lives at sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kunigseq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The people of the underworld asked that when he returned to earth he send them ice, 'for we thirst for cold water down here.' Back on earth, his son soon fell sick and died; Kunigseq no longer cared to live, having seen what the underworld was like. He caught a guillemot, then a raven, ate them one after the other, and died — and they threw his body out into the sea. The tale encodes the angakok seance in which the shaman visits the land of the dead and returns as messenger for his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kunigseq'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman Who Had a Bear as a Foster-Son

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son', eBook #28932

summary.en: An old woman thaws a frozen bear cub and raises it on blubber, teaching it human speech and hunting manners; with a plaited-sinew collar as its mark, it becomes an unbeatable seal-hunter that men can recognize and spare. After it hauls home the corpse of the one man who would not spare it, the foster-mother sends her bear away to its own kin, and far north, when bears are abroad, an iceberg-sized bear with a black smudged spot on its side is still seen.
summary.zh: 老嫗將凍僵的熊崽置於晾架解凍，以脂油哺育，教以人言與獵禮；頸繫筋辮項圈為記，成為無人能勝的海豹獵手，見圈者皆放行。熊拖回不肯留情者之屍後，養母泣遣其返北地親族。自今北境熊群出沒時，猶有巨如冰山、脅染黑漬之熊現身。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Includes killing of a reckless outsider hunter as told in the source; presented as archival narrative.

passages.text: An old woman lived nearest the shore and was fed by the hunters above. They brought home a whole bear, and its killer's wife asked through the window whether she would like the cub. She warmed the frozen cub on the drying frame, fed it on greaves and melted blubber, and it lay beside her at night and grew fast. Talking to it in human speech, she gave it a human mind: when it wanted food it sniffed. The children played with it — 'Little bear, remember to sheathe your claws' — until it grew stronger than grown men and the hunters took it out to find seal, telling it to keep down wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Hunters from the north nearly killed the bear; its rescuers begged the old woman to give it a mark by which it might be known, and she made it a collar of plaited sinews as broad as a harpoon line. Thenceforth it never failed to catch seal, stronger than the strongest hunter and never staying home even in the worst weather, though never bigger than an ordinary bear. All the villages knew the collar, and though hunters sometimes came close, they let it go on sight. When men from beyond Angmagssalik vowed to kill the uncatchable bear, the elders forbade it: the foster-mother could ill manage without its help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One stormy evening the bear came home and sprang to its bench, and the old woman found outside the body of a dead man it had hauled home — the man from the north, who had run so fast he had thrown off his furs; his comrades, said the report, had urged the bear to resist him, because he would not leave it alone. Long after, the old foster-mother told the bear it must leave her, or it would be killed, and wept as she said it; the bear pressed its muzzle to the floor and wept too. One morning with no cloud as big as a hand in the sky, she smeared oil and soot on her hands and stroked its side unseen. It sniffed at her and went. Far to the north, when many bears are abroad, there sometimes comes a bear as big as an iceberg, with a black spot on its side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives', eBook #28932

summary.en: The fattener-of-wives Imarasugssuaq feeds each bride nothing but salmon and no water, until she is too heavy to flee and he kills and eats her. His newest wife, Misana, sister of many brothers, licks drifted snow to thin herself, stuffs her clothes into a dummy that shrieks when harpooned, and escapes through a hole behind the house; changing herself into a piece of wood by amulet, she evades his knife and reaches her brothers, who hold him fast so she may kill him.
summary.zh: 食妻者伊馬拉舒亞克每娶新婦，僅以鮭肉飼之，滴水不予，待其肥重難逃，便殺而食之。新妻米薩納——眾兄弟之妹——趁夫外出舐雪瘦身，以衣絮充假人騙其魚叉，又唸護身符化為木塊避刃，逃歸兄弟之家。眾人縛住那食妻者，讓她親手復仇。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Domestic-violence and cannibalism motifs presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: The great Imarasugssuaq was wont to eat his wives. He fattened them, giving them nothing but salmon to eat and nothing at all to drink. Once when he had lost a wife in the usual way, he took Misana, the sister of many brothers, and began fattening her as usual. One day, grown so fat she could hardly move, she managed to tumble down from the bench, crawl to the entrance, and lick the snow that had drifted in; licking and licking, she felt herself lighter. Whenever her husband was out in his kayak she licked up snow, until she could once more move about freely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day she stuffed out her breeches and tunic until they looked like a real human being behind the lamp, and instructed the dummy: when my husband comes and tells you to come out, answer 'I cannot move because I am grown so fat'; and when he comes in and harpoons you, shriek as if in pain. She dug a hole at the back of the house and crept in. The husband returned, harpooned the dummy wife with his great bird-spear, heard it shriek and fall — but found no blood, only stuffed-out clothes. Searching, he chased the fleeing woman; seeing him closing, she said 'Now I remember, my amulet is a piece of wood,' and changed into wood at once. He stabbed the piece once or twice; she felt only a stinging pain. When he left to fetch his axe, she changed back and fled to her brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Hiding behind the skin hangings at her brothers' house, she heard her husband approach, weeping over his lost wife. In the evening the many brothers sang mockery at him — 'Men say that Imarasugssuaq eats his wives' — and she answered from behind the hangings: 'I said it, and I ran away because you tried to kill me.' The brothers fell upon him and held him fast so that his wife might kill him. She took her knife, but each time she tried to strike it only grazed his skin, for her fingers lost their power. While she stood there trying in vain to stab him, they saw that he was already dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives'; not verbatim.

title.en: Qalaganguase, Who Passed to the Land of Ghosts
title.zh: 入幽靈之地的卡拉康瓦塞

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts', eBook #28932

summary.en: Lame and orphaned, Qalaganguase is left behind when the village goes hunting — and the ghosts come in to play: wrestling, telling stories, drinking from the water tub, even his dead sister among them. Promised his strength again if he tells no tales, he blurts out the visit to the returning hunters and the strength drains away. At last his dead parents lead him out of the house to the land of ghosts, and he passes over, becoming (so it is said) a woman among the dead.
summary.zh: 跛足孤兒卡拉康瓦塞被村人棄於屋中——幽靈成群而入，角力講古、舀水而飲，亡姊亦在其中。幽靈允諾守秘者可復得氣力；他向歸獵者吐實，氣力隨之流逝。最後亡父亡母引他出屋，渡往幽靈之地；據云他化為女子，村人自此不復見之。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland ghost-land narrative recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Gender transformation of the dead presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Qalaganguase's parents ate seaweed and died of it; then his one sister died, and only strangers looked after the boy, whose lower body was dead so that he could not walk. Left alone while the village hunted, he heard a sound and dragged himself, in great pain, into the next house to hide behind the skin hangings. In walked a ghost — 'Ai! There are people here!' It drank from the water tub, emptying the dipper twice, thanked the thirsty one for the drink as it used to drink when it lived on earth, and went out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another day, left alone again, he heard the walls and frame of the house shake, and a crowd of ghosts came tumbling in, one after the other — the last one his sister, dead but a little time before. The ghosts sat on the floor and played: they wrestled, told stories, laughed all night. At first afraid, Qalaganguase found the company pleasant. When the hunters were heard returning, the ghosts hastened away: 'Now mind you do not tell tales; if you do as we say, you will gain strength again, and there will be nothing you cannot do.' His sister could hardly slip out because her brother's touch stayed her — the hunters could just see a pair of vanishing feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'The house has been full of people, and they made the night pass pleasantly for me,' said Qalaganguase, already feeling his strength return — but hardly had he spoken when the strength slowly left him. The villagers tied the lame boy to a frame post and let him swing, trying to beat the drum, and then went off to a singing contest, leaving him behind. There his dead mother and father came in and asked why he was alone. 'I am lame,' he said, 'and they left me behind.' 'Come away with us.' 'It is better so, perhaps,' said the boy, and they bore him to the land of ghosts. It is said he became a woman when they changed him to a ghost, and his fellow-villagers never saw him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts'; not verbatim.
